title: Introverts and Extroverts
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: In everyday speech, people are often described as introverts or extroverts. The terms were popularised by the Swiss psychiatrist Carl Jung in the 1920s, who used them to describe where a person gets energy: extroverts feel energised by company and activity, while introverts feel energised by time alone and by reflection. The distinction has since become one of the most widely used ideas in psychology, but it is also one of the most misunderstood, and the popular picture of the two types is often a caricature. Understanding what the words really mean can help both individuals and organisations to make better decisions about work, study and friendship.

The first misunderstanding is that introverts are shy. Shyness is a fear of social judgement, while introversion is a preference for less stimulation. An introvert may be perfectly confident when speaking to a large audience, and then need a quiet hour to recover. A shy extrovert, on the other hand, may long for company but be too anxious to seek it. The two qualities often occur together, but they are separate, and mixing them up can lead to unhelpful advice.

Research suggests that personality is better described as a spectrum than as two types. Most people lie somewhere in the middle and are sometimes called ambiverts, behaving as introverts in some situations and extroverts in others. Surveys in several countries find that the great majority of people score in the middle range, and that very high or very low scores are uncommon. Nevertheless, the labels remain useful, since they describe real differences in preference, even if they are not sharp dividing lines.

Where do these differences come from? Studies of twins suggest that about half of the variation in extroversion is inherited. Some researchers believe that introverts have brains that react more strongly to stimulation, so that busy places tire them faster. Others emphasise upbringing and culture. In some cultures, outgoing behaviour is admired and encouraged, while in others, quiet reflection is valued more. Whatever the cause, it is clear that personality cannot be entirely changed, though people can learn to act differently when necessary.

Schools and workplaces often favour extroverts. Classroom teaching rewards pupils who speak up, and many offices are open-plan, with noise and constant interruptions. The writer Susan Cain argued in a popular book that this wastes the talents of the quieter half of the population, who may be better at listening, at concentrating for long periods, and at thinking before acting. Critics reply that the evidence for such differences is weaker than she suggests and that some of her claims go further than the research allows.

Employers have tried different solutions. Some companies offer quiet rooms where staff can work without interruption, while others allow long periods of working from home. Team leaders are encouraged to let people prepare before meetings, instead of asking for instant opinions. Dr Rosa Almeida, an organisational psychologist, says that the best teams include both types and that the key to success is for the leader to recognise how each member works best, instead of requiring all to behave in the same way.

At an individual level, understanding one's own preferences can be valuable. An introvert who knows that crowded events are tiring can plan time to recover afterwards, while an extrovert who finds long periods alone difficult can arrange to meet friends. The aim is not to change one's personality but to build a life that suits it. As Dr Almeida puts it, 'neither type is better; each is a different way of being at one's best.' It is a reminder that people differ in ways that are worth respecting.
